prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach a new regime of measurement precision

statement.case_for: I opened with spherical-aberration correction (B053) because it is my own field, and I said then that this closeness obliges me to hold it to a strict standard. Having read all eight ballots I move the optical lattice clock (B027) to first place. It is the only candidate that seven of eight members ranked and that five placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with very different backgrounds: atomic physics (Lindroth, Kroll), condensed matter (Eriksson), instrumentation (Pearce) and quantum devices (Johansson). That breadth matters less to me than the record. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and his first strontium lattice demonstration are the original invention, and Ye's group then showed that the concept delivers uncertainties near 1e-18 and many-body clock physics. The result has been checked by independent clock comparisons at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL, so it is experimentally verified in the sense I demand. It opens a door: tests of fundamental constants and the gravitational redshift over millimetres, relativistic geodesy, and a basis for redefining the second. The two names match the invention-plus-development story that colleagues reported independently, without much dispute.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize covered ion control and ion clock technology (Wineland), and Ye's career sits close to both. I also worry that Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and other early clock groups are left out, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a prize could be argued as either well timed or slightly early. Separately, in giving up B053 I am setting aside a case in which I know the instruments well: Rose and Haider designed the correctors, Urban led the first working corrected TEM, and the effect on materials science is huge. My own ballot shows that attribution is not clean there, because Krivanek's corrected-STEM work is outside the credited names.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B053 first together with me, arguing that Rose, Haider and Urban form a natural three-way split (optical design, hexapole corrector, Julich implementation) while acknowledging that Krivanek's quadrupole-octupole correctors have claims the credited list omits.
responses.response: We two are the only members who put B053 first, and we are the two members closest to instrument-driven measurement, which is a reason to discount our agreement rather than count it. I agree the Rose-Haider-Urban split is natural for the 1998 TEM demonstration, but you flag the Krivanek problem yourself, and I share it: a corrected STEM that produced atomic-resolution spectroscopy was an independent route to the same limit, and our committee cannot be absolutely sure it has found the people who did the original work while one lineage is left out. I would keep B053 as the principal alternative and want the record on TEM versus STEM correction examined before anyone asks for it to be taken forward. I also notice you ranked B027 third with a clean attribution, so I hope you can accept it as the lead.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B027 first because it turns an atomic-structure insight (Lamb-Dicke trapping with cancelled light shifts) into a new level of precision, with Katori proposing the magic-wavelength scheme and Ye's group driving performance, and she notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes only partly cover neighbouring ground.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your argument and want to qualify one part. The magic-wavelength condition is the original idea, and a discovery-or-invention prize should be anchored there, so Katori's name is the firmest in the configuration. Ye's claim rests on bringing the strontium clock to the highest precision and on the many-body and spin-exchange developments, which is a development case rather than the original invention. That is still decisive in my view, but the citation should say invention and development, so that nobody reads it as a second-best-experiment prize of the kind I would resist. I would also like your view on whether the Takamoto, Ludlow and Hall contributions you mention are strong enough to raise a real attribution problem or only a footnote.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked the topological insulator trio (B057) first as a clear, verified discovery where band-structure theory predicts the outcome quantitatively, with Kane and Mele providing the Z2 classification and Molenkamp the HgTe measurement.
responses.response: I put B057 fourth and I respect the science, but I have two reservations that you under-weigh. First, the credited names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe prediction is what Molenkamp's experiment actually tested, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Hasan and others; for a committee that must be sure of the original contributors this is a bigger gap than your ballot suggests. Second, the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions means we must explain what is new here, which is possible but not free. I do not dismiss the case: it is my second alternative, and if the credited set could be justified I would take it seriously as a rival to the clock. For now it has too many open attribution questions to lead.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B027 first as the clearest case on the list of a measurement technique that changed what can be measured, noting that atom numbers, removal of Doppler and recoil shifts, and 1e-18 uncertainty have opened redefinition of the second, geodesy and dark-matter searches, and that the two-person prize is clean.
responses.response: I agree, and the point about changing what can be measured is the one that persuades me, because it is the same standard I apply to electron optics. Where I would add caution is on the downstream uses: geodesy and dark-matter searches are promises of the door opening, not results, so the citation should rest on the demonstrated accuracy and comparisons rather than on applications. I would also ask you, as an experimentalist in the same area, whether the two-name configuration should hold if Ye's contribution is judged as development of Katori's concept; if you see a third name who contributed an original experiment, the committee should hear it now.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's role is original invention or decisive development of Katori's concept, and whether the citation should be worded to reflect that distinction.
Whether another early lattice-clock group (Takamoto and colleagues, Lemonde, Ludlow or others) has an attribution claim strong enough to disturb the two-name configuration.

How much the 2005 and 2012 prizes (frequency comb, ion clocks) overlap with the credited work in the committee's eyes, and whether the redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or a reason to act.
For B053, whether Krivanek's corrected-STEM work, not in the credited names, is an independent original contribution; I cannot settle this from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from my profile for B027, B057 or the other shortlisted candidates. For B053 I should be open that spherical-aberration correction is my own field of transmission electron microscopy, I currently serve as IFSM president, and my microscopy community overlaps with the corrector developers' world, although my profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Rose, Haider or Urban; the committee may wish to consider this if B053 advances. Also, Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and works on circuit QED (B036), which the committee should note when weighing our views, but I have no personal stake there.
